2027-06-23.title: Wednesday of the Twelfth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: He believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness
The Lord remembers his covenant for ever (or: Alleluia)
You will know them by their fruits
2027-06-23.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 12 (Year I). Liturgical colour: green. This evening the Vigil Mass of the Nativity of St John the Baptist may be celebrated (white), with its own readings: Jeremiah 1:4–10 (“Before I formed you in the womb I knew you”); Psalm 71:1–2, 3–4a, 5–6ab, 15ab, 17; 1 Peter 1:8–12; Luke 1:5–17, the angel's announcement to Zechariah in the Temple.
2027-06-23.verse: He brought him outside and said, “Look toward heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” Then he said to him, “So shall your descendants be.” And he believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness.
theo: Some years have passed since Abram left Haran, and the great promise has not moved. He is rich, respected and still childless. Then “the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision, ‘Do not be afraid, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great.’” And for the first time in the Bible we hear Abram answer God with a complaint: “O Lord GOD, what will you give me, for I continue childless, and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?” What use is a reward if there is no son to inherit it? The Bible is not afraid of such honest prayers. God does not rebuke him. He takes him outside under the night sky of the desert: “Look toward heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” Then he said to him, “So shall your descendants be.” Nothing in Abram's tent has changed. Sarai is still old and childless. But Abram looks up from his problem to God's sky, and the most important sentence of the chapter follows: “And he believed the LORD; and the LORD reckoned it to him as righteousness.” St Paul will build his teaching on this verse: we are made right with God not by our own achievements but by trusting his promise (Romans 4:3; Galatians 3:6), a faith that, as St James adds, shows itself in works (James 2:22–23). Then God seals the promise with a strange ceremony. Abram brings a heifer, a goat, a ram, a turtledove and a pigeon, cuts the animals in two and lays the halves opposite each other. In the ancient world the two parties to a treaty walked between such pieces, as if to say: may I be cut in two like these if I break my word (compare Jeremiah 34:18). Abram waits all day, driving away the birds of prey. At sunset a deep sleep falls on him, and a terrifying darkness. And then “a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces.” Only God passes through. Abram does not. God binds himself alone to his promise. “On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram.” The Psalm sings the same faithfulness: “He is mindful of his covenant forever, of the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations, the covenant that he made with Abraham.” The Church teaches that this covenant with the Jewish people has never been revoked, “for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29; Catechism 121).

In the Gospel Jesus warns his disciples about a danger every generation meets: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves.” How can we tell them apart? Jesus gives one simple test, said twice: “You will know them by their fruits.” “Are grapes gathered from thorns, or figs from thistles? In the same way, every good tree bears good fruit, but the bad tree bears bad fruit.” A preacher may be eloquent, a video may draw millions of views, a healing service may be crowded; the question is still the fruit. Does this message lead to humility or to pride, to charity or to money, to unity with the Church or to division, to repentance or to excitement only? St Paul named the fruit of the Spirit: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Abram's faith was not just a feeling under the stars; its fruit was a whole life of obedience. And tomorrow the Church celebrates the birth of the greatest of the prophets, St John the Baptist, a true prophet whose fruit was this: he pointed away from himself to Christ. This evening, in many parishes, the Vigil Mass of his Nativity is celebrated. Its first reading is the call of Jeremiah, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you,” and its Gospel is the angel's message to the old priest Zechariah in the Temple: your prayer has been heard, and Elizabeth will bear a son, “and you will name him John.” Abram looking at the stars and Zechariah hearing the angel are two old men to whom God says the same thing: nothing is impossible for him.
outline: Ask: when was the last time you told God honestly what disappointed you?
Abram's honest complaint and God's answer under the night sky.
Point 2 · He believed, and it was reckoned as righteousness
Faith that trusts the promise, and the covenant God alone signs.
How to tell true prophets from false, and the true prophet whose birth we celebrate tomorrow.
“He believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness.”
live: Tonight, if the monsoon clouds allow, step outside for a minute and look at the sky; if not, look at a picture of it. Tell God the promise you are still waiting for, and say: I believe.
Before forwarding a religious message or video this week, ask: does it lead to love, humility and unity with the Church? If not, do not pass it on.
2027-06-23.prayer: Lord God, you said to Abram: do not be afraid, I am your shield. When we are tired of waiting and the promise seems far away, lead us outside to look at your sky, and give us faith like his, which you reckoned as righteousness. You alone passed between the pieces and bound yourself to your covenant; keep us faithful to the new covenant in the blood of your Son. Protect us from false prophets, and make our lives bear the good fruit of your Spirit. As we prepare to celebrate the birth of St John the Baptist, prepare our hearts for Christ. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: At the consecration the priest says over the chalice: this is the chalice of my Blood, the Blood of the new and eternal covenant. The God who passed alone between the pieces to bind himself to Abram has in Christ bound himself to us for ever, not with the blood of animals but with the Blood of his Son. Every Mass is that covenant renewed and made present.

quick: Abram complains honestly that he is still childless; God takes him outside and tells him to count the stars: so shall your descendants be.
Abram believed the Lord, and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness; God seals the covenant by passing alone between the pieces as a smoking fire pot and flaming torch.
Jesus warns against false prophets in sheep's clothing: you will know them by their fruits.
2027-06-23.action: Tell God honestly about a promise you are still waiting for, and make an act of faith in him.
2027-06-23.question: What fruit does my faith bear in my daily life?

family.explain: Abram was sad because he had no children. One night God took him outside and said: look at the sky! Can you count the stars? Your family will be as many as the stars. Abram could not see how it could happen, but he believed God. And God was very pleased with his faith. Jesus also said: a good tree gives good fruit. When we believe in God, our lives should be full of good fruit, like kindness and patience.
family.intention: We pray for couples who long for children, and for all who are waiting for a promise of God to come true.
family.ask: Ask: “What good fruit can each of us show this week at home?” Then, if the sky is clear, go out together and count the stars.

illus: A couple in Kannur waited eleven years for a child. Friends offered advice, relatives asked questions, and some well-meaning people gave them the numbers of preachers who promised a baby within a year for a donation. The wife said later that what kept her faith alive was not those promises but an old priest who told her to read Genesis 15 every night for a month and simply say, like Abram: I believe. Their son was born in the twelfth year. She says she would have kept believing even if he had not been, because she had learned to look at the stars and not only at her own tent. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord God, you are our shield and our great reward. Increase our faith, keep us faithful to your covenant, and make our lives bear good fruit. Amen.
share: O Lord God, what will you give me? (Genesis 15:2). What disappointment do I need to bring honestly to God in prayer?
He believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6). When has trusting God's promise changed the way I live?
You will know them by their fruits (Matthew 7:20). What fruit are others seeing in my life?
pm.resp: The Lord remembers his covenant for ever.
interc: For the Church, that her faith in God's promises may never grow tired.
For the Jewish people, the children of Abraham, to whom God's covenant and promises belong.
For couples longing for a child, and for all who wait for an answer from God.
For all preachers and teachers of the faith, that their words and lives may bear good fruit, and for those misled by false prophets.
For our group, that as we prepare for the birth of St John the Baptist, we may become heralds of Christ.
pm.close: Father, you remember your covenant for ever. Make us children of Abraham by faith, and fruitful trees in your garden. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, Abram had left everything at God's word, and years later he still had no child. So he says to God: what will you give me, for I continue childless? (Genesis 15:2). It is a very honest prayer. Many of us have prayed like that: Lord, I have done everything you asked, and still I am waiting.

God does not scold him. He takes him outside and says: look toward heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them. So shall your descendants be (Genesis 15:5). Nothing had changed in Abram's tent. But he lifted his eyes from his problem to God's sky. And he believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6). This is faith: not seeing, but trusting the One who promises.

Then God makes a covenant. In those days, people who made a treaty walked between animals cut in two, as if to say: may this happen to me if I break my word. But that night only God passes between the pieces, as a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch. God binds himself alone. His faithfulness does not depend on ours. The Psalm sings: he is mindful of his covenant forever (Psalm 105:8).

In the Gospel Jesus says: beware of false prophets; you will know them by their fruits (Matthew 7:15–16). Not every attractive preacher is a true prophet. Look at the fruit: love, humility, peace, unity. Tomorrow we celebrate the birth of John the Baptist, a true prophet, whose fruit was to point to Jesus. This evening many parishes begin the feast with the Vigil Mass. Let us also prepare: lift up our eyes like Abram, believe God's promise, and let our faith bear good fruit. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever tried to count the stars at night? You cannot, there are too many! God told Abram: your family will be as many as the stars. Abram was old and had no children, but he believed God. And God kept his promise. Jesus said: a good tree gives good fruit. When we believe in God, we should give good fruit too: being kind, sharing, saying sorry. Tonight, look up at the sky and say: God, I believe you!

intro: Theme: “He believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness.”
An honest complaint, a sky full of stars, a covenant God signs alone, and the fruit by which true faith is known.

sub: Do not be afraid, I am your shield.
q: He brought him outside and said, “Look toward heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” Then he said to him, “So shall your descendants be.”
Therefore from one person, and this one as good as dead, descendants were born, “as many as the stars of heaven and as the innumerable grains of sand by the seashore.”
points.apply: Bring God one honest disappointment in prayer today, and end with Abram's act of faith: I believe.

sub: The pieces and the birds of prey.
q: He is mindful of his covenant forever, of the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations,
For what does the scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.”
points.apply: At the consecration this week, thank God that his covenant with you rests on his faithfulness, not on your strength.

points.h: You will know them by their fruits
sub: Grapes are not gathered from thorns.
The true prophet points to Christ.
q: They are like trees planted by streams of water, which yield their fruit in its season, and their leaves do not wither. In all that they do, they prosper.
By contrast, the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control.
points.apply: Test one religious message you receive this week by its fruit before you believe it or share it.

concl: Abram believed God's promise under the stars, and God bound himself to Abram in a covenant he alone sealed.
True faith bears good fruit; tomorrow's feast shows us John the Baptist, the true prophet who pointed to Christ.
2027-06-23.resolve: Make an act of faith each night this week, and ask God to show you one fruit of his Spirit to grow in.
